opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the experiential paradigm starts from a very simple observation: an agent lives in a stream of experience. It takes actions, it receives observations, and it gets rewards. That's all there is, really, from the agent's point of view. Sensation, action, reward, flowing on and on through time. And intelligence, in that view, is the ability to adjust your actions so as to increase the reward you get in that stream. That's what it means to have a goal and to be good at achieving it.

Now, knowledge, then, has to be about that stream. If I say I know something, what I really mean, ultimately, is that I can predict something about what will happen in my experience. If I know that this cup is on the table, that means if I reach out in a certain way, I'll feel a certain thing. If I turn my head, I'll see a certain thing. So knowledge is predictive. It's statements about the stream of experience, about what will happen if you do certain things.

And that's really important, because it means knowledge can be tested. You can check it against your experience. You make a prediction, then you see what actually happens, and you learn from the difference. That's very different from the large language model approach, where the knowledge is about what a person would say. There's no ground truth there in the same sense. There's no sense in which the system does something and then finds out whether it was right about the world. It's mimicking people who had experience, but it isn't having the experience itself.

So in the experiential paradigm, you have the policy, which is what to do; you have the value function, which is how well things are going; you have a model of the world, which is your predictive knowledge about what will happen; and you have your perception, your representation of state. All of these are learned from experience, and all of them are continually improved from experience as you go. Intelligence isn't something you build in up front and then freeze. It's something that grows as you live, as you interact with the world. That's the essence of it, I think.

r001.rationale: It defines intelligence as adjusting actions to increase the reward received in the stream of experience.

r002.rationale: It says knowledge is predictive: what will happen in experience, including what follows from particular actions.

r003.rationale: It explains that predictions can be checked against experience by observing what actually happens and comparing it with the prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key move is that everything has to be grounded in experience. By experience I mean the signals that actually come in and go out of the agent: the observations it receives, the actions it takes, and the rewards. That's the data. That's all the agent ever has access to. So if we're going to talk about knowledge, it has to be knowledge about that stream, knowledge about what will happen in experience.

So intelligence, in this view, is the computational part of the ability to achieve goals. And the goal is given by the reward signal. The agent is trying to get more reward over time, and the way it does that is by building up knowledge, predictions about how its experience will unfold depending on what it does.

Knowledge, then, is predictive. It's statements about the future of the experiential stream. Not "the chair is in the room" as some abstract proposition, but "if I move this way, I will see such and such, I will feel such and such." Everything that we would call knowledge of the world has to cash out, eventually, in predictions about sensations and the consequences of actions. If it doesn't, I would say it's not really knowledge, it's just a symbol floating free.

And the great advantage of that is that knowledge of this kind can be verified by the agent itself. It makes a prediction, it waits, it sees what happens, and it compares. It doesn't need a human to come along and tell it whether it's right. That's what you need for an agent to learn continually and open-endedly, without a designer putting the knowledge in by hand. The agent can check its own knowledge against experience, correct it, and keep going.

So within the experiential paradigm, intelligence is this ongoing process of learning from the stream, building up a model in terms of predictions, using that model to choose actions that lead to more reward, and continually revising it as new experience comes in. Everything comes from the data, and everything is accountable to the data.

r001.rationale: It describes intelligence as pursuing more reward over time by using a model to choose actions, within an ongoing process of learning from experience.

r002.rationale: It directly defines knowledge as predictions about how the future experiential stream will unfold.

r003.rationale: It says the agent checks a prediction by waiting for what happens and comparing the result with the prediction.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that an agent has a stream of experience: observations coming in, actions going out, and rewards. Intelligence is the ability to use that experience to achieve goals—to learn how the world works and how to act effectively in it.

Then knowledge has to connect back to that stream. If I say I know something about the world, what am I predicting I would experience? And under what actions? Knowing that a door opens means, in part, predicting what will happen if I turn the handle and push. It’s a prediction conditioned on a way of behaving.

That gives knowledge an operational meaning. The agent can test its expectations against what actually happens and improve them. And it can learn those expectations at many timescales, from what happens in the next fraction of a second to what happens over an extended course of action.

The important thing is that we don’t have to begin by supplying the agent with a human description of the world. We want it to develop its own understanding through experience, with its predictions and its success at achieving goals providing the grounding.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence uses experience to achieve goals and act effectively, but it does not clearly characterize intelligence as modifying actions to increase rewards.

r002.rationale: It describes knowledge as predicting what the agent will experience, including how those predictions depend on its actions.

r003.rationale: It says the agent can test its expectations against what actually happens and improve them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is that an agent has a stream of experience: observations coming in, actions going out, and rewards indicating how well things are going. Intelligence is the ability to learn from that experience so as to achieve goals more effectively.

Knowledge, in this view, should also be grounded in experience. If I say I know something, I ought to be able to say what difference it makes to what I expect to experience. What would happen if I took this action? What would I observe if I followed this course of behavior? Those are predictions, and they can be tested against what actually happens.

That gives us a way to think about knowledge beyond a collection of facts expressed in language. An agent can know how to get somewhere, how an object will behave, or what consequences a choice will have. And it can continually revise that knowledge through interaction. The important thing is the connection back to experience: that’s what gives the knowledge its meaning, and that’s how the agent can find out whether it’s right.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence learns from experience to achieve goals more effectively, but does not clearly characterize it as modifying actions to increase rewards.

r002.rationale: It grounds knowledge in predictions about what the agent will observe and how experience will unfold.

r003.rationale: It says predictions can be tested against what actually happens.
